projects.name: Huddle
projects.headline: A campus of possibilities. One live map.
projects.summary: A geospatial event-discovery platform for the UMD community. I designed, built, and launched the full stack, from real-time discovery to concurrency-safe RSVPs.
projects.role: Founder & Lead Engineer · Solo full-stack development
projects.imageAlt: Huddle's live website, showing campus event discovery and an illustrated event map
projects.intro: Finding something to do on campus should not mean searching through disconnected group chats. Huddle brings local events onto a live map, with the infrastructure to discover an event, reserve a spot, and keep a community connected.

challenge.title: The hard part is keeping everything consistent.
challenge.body: A live map is only one part of the product. Capacity limits, waitlists, attendance records, and public event data all need to agree—even when people act at the same time. I owned the application end to end, including its 68 pages, API layer, data model, security rules, and deployment.

architecture.caption: A simplified view of Huddle's production architecture.

nodes.label: Discover
nodes.detail: Map-based discovery with geohash-indexed events and real-time Firestore listeners.

nodes.label: Coordinate
nodes.detail: Authentication, event workflows, and transactional capacity checks.

nodes.label: Persist
nodes.detail: Atomic writes, access-controlled attendee records, and tested security rules.

nodes.label: Assist
nodes.detail: Event generation with structured output and validation before it reaches users.

decisions.title: One transaction. A consistent RSVP.
decisions.problem: Independent capacity checks and writes can race when multiple attendees request the last spot.
decisions.decision: Consolidated capacity checks, waitlist promotions, and badge awards into one atomic Firestore transaction.
decisions.result: Eliminated RSVP race conditions under concurrent load.

decisions.title: Send only what the public needs.
decisions.problem: Public event responses carried unnecessary fields, and attendee data needed stronger separation.
decisions.decision: Introduced field allowlists and moved 566 live attendee records into access-controlled subcollections, with a verification script for the migration.
decisions.result: Reduced payload size from 11 KB to 1.5 KB per event—an 87% reduction—with no data lost in the migration.

decisions.title: Make background work predictable.
decisions.problem: Five separate cron jobs and full collection scans added unnecessary operational work.
decisions.decision: Consolidated jobs into a fault-isolated dispatcher, removed full collection scans, and added emulator-based security-rule tests with CI gating.
decisions.result: A simpler scheduled-work pipeline and automated checks around data access.

decisions.title: Treat model output as untrusted input.
decisions.problem: Generated event content needs to be safe for the product to consume; a successful model response alone is not enough.
decisions.decision: Constrained Gemini event generation to a structured schema and validated generations before presenting them to users.
decisions.result: AI assistance sits inside the application's validation boundary.

projects.outcome: Shipped a live platform serving campus users, with 565+ events, 48 API routes, and 68 pages. The work spans product delivery, concurrency, data access, performance, and operations.
projects.reflection: The most valuable work was often below the interface: choosing the transaction boundary, limiting public data, and making migrations verifiable. Those decisions are what let the product evolve with confidence.

projects.name: ClassNest
projects.headline: From lecture notes to learning moments.
projects.summary: An AI-powered learning management system that turns PDF lecture material into quizzes, supported by a tested Django backend and a React interface.
projects.intro: Creating quizzes from lecture material takes time away from teaching. ClassNest explores how a learning management system can automate that work by connecting uploaded PDFs to an LLM-powered quiz-generation pipeline.

challenge.title: Connect AI capability to working software.
challenge.body: The challenge was not just getting a model to generate questions. The pipeline had to fit into a full-stack learning application, with a database, a user interface, repeatable builds, and tests across the backend and frontend.

nodes.label: Upload
nodes.detail: Lecture documents provide the source material for quiz generation.

nodes.label: Orchestrate
nodes.detail: The application connects document input with the model-backed generation pipeline.

nodes.label: Generate
nodes.detail: An LLM converts lecture content into quiz questions.

nodes.label: Learn
nodes.detail: The learning application presents quizzes and stores application data.

decisions.title: Integrate the model into a complete workflow.
decisions.problem: Manually translating lecture PDFs into quizzes is repetitive work for educators.
decisions.decision: Built a Python pipeline using Llama3 through the Groq API, integrated with Django and React.
decisions.result: Automated the conversion from uploaded lecture material to quizzes.

decisions.title: Test across the application boundary.
decisions.problem: A working generation demo does not establish confidence in the surrounding application.
decisions.decision: Used test-driven development with unit and integration tests across Django services and React components.
decisions.result: Enforced 90% test coverage across the application.

decisions.title: Make delivery reproducible.
decisions.problem: The application combines frontend, backend, database, and external model dependencies.
decisions.decision: Containerized the application with Docker and shipped through CI/CD.
decisions.result: A repeatable path from development to delivery.

projects.outcome: Delivered an end-to-end learning application with automated PDF-to-quiz generation, Docker packaging, CI/CD, and 90% test coverage.
projects.reflection: Code coverage measures the application, not the quality of generated questions. A next step would be a curated evaluation set for factual accuracy and question quality, alongside explicit inference-failure tests.

projects.name: Smart Health Monitor
projects.headline: Making vital signs visible, remotely.
projects.summary: A sensor-to-dashboard prototype for remote patient vitals tracking, connecting five hardware sensors with real-time monitoring and threshold-based alerts.
projects.intro: This project connected physical sensors to a software monitoring interface, exploring how patient vitals could be tracked remotely with timely threshold-based alerts.

challenge.title: Bridge the physical and digital systems.
challenge.body: The core work was integrating five hardware sensors, moving readings through Arduino and Raspberry Pi components, and making the data visible in a real-time dashboard. This was a monitoring prototype.

architecture.caption: A simplified view of the monitoring prototype.

nodes.label: Connect
nodes.detail: Connect hardware readings to the software system.

nodes.label: Monitor
nodes.detail: Show incoming readings and surface threshold-based alerts.

decisions.title: Bring the signals into one view.
decisions.problem: Readings from separate sensors need a shared interface to be useful for remote monitoring.
decisions.decision: Integrated five sensors into a real-time dashboard using Python, Arduino, and Raspberry Pi.
decisions.result: Enabled remote vitals tracking with threshold-based alerts.

projects.outcome: Demonstrated a sensor-to-dashboard workflow for remote monitoring and alerts.
projects.reflection: This project shaped my interest in the interfaces between systems: how data moves, how it becomes useful, and how software connects to real-world needs.
